label: Parameter Estimation
notes: This appendix spans printed pages 568 through 577 and underpins every gold-standard method in the book. We frame estimation as recovering parameters from noisy measurements, then derive why minimizing geometric reprojection error is the principled choice rather than a convenient heuristic.

label: The Measurement Model
notes: Everything starts with a model: measurements equal a deterministic function of the parameters plus random noise. Fixing the noise distribution is what converts a vague fitting problem into a well-posed statistical one, and it dictates which cost function we should actually minimize.

label: Maximum Likelihood
notes: Maximum likelihood selects the parameters that make the observed data most probable. For independent isotropic Gaussian noise the log-likelihood reduces to a negative sum of squared residuals, so the maximum likelihood estimate is exactly the least-squares minimizer of geometric error.

label: Likelihood Surface and the MLE
notes: The likelihood is a surface over parameter space whose peak is the maximum likelihood estimate. Curvature at that peak controls how sharply the data pin the parameters; a broad flat ridge signals a poorly conditioned or near-degenerate estimation problem.

label: MAP and Bayesian Estimation
notes: A prior multiplies the likelihood to give a posterior, and its mode is the maximum a posteriori estimate. The prior pulls the solution away from the raw maximum likelihood point toward prior belief, while full Bayesian estimation keeps the whole posterior instead of one number.

label: Bias and Variance
notes: We judge an estimator by two quantities: bias measures systematic offset of its average from the truth, variance measures its scatter under resampling. Mean squared error decomposes into both, so a slightly biased estimator can still beat an unbiased but high-variance competitor.

label: Fisher Information
notes: The Fisher information matrix is the expected curvature of the log-likelihood, equivalently the variance of the score. Large Fisher information means the likelihood is sharply peaked and the data are highly informative about the parameters, which is the quantity the Cramer-Rao bound depends on.

label: The Cramer-Rao Lower Bound
notes: The Cramer-Rao bound states that any unbiased estimator has covariance no smaller than the inverse Fisher information. It sets a hard floor on achievable precision; an estimator that meets it is efficient, and maximum likelihood attains it asymptotically as samples grow.

label: Algebraic vs Geometric Error
notes: Linear algorithms minimize an algebraic residual that is fast but lacks statistical meaning and weights points unevenly. Geometric or reprojection error measures true image-plane distance, so its minimizer is the maximum likelihood estimate under Gaussian image noise and is the gold standard.

label: Nuisance Parameters
notes: Triangulation and reconstruction carry nuisance parameters such as the unknown scene points that we must estimate but do not ultimately care about. They inflate the problem dimension yet are essential; profiling or marginalizing them yields a correct covariance for the parameters we want.

label: Why the Gold Standard
notes: Putting the pieces together: the Gaussian measurement model makes maximum likelihood equal to least-squares geometric error, the Cramer-Rao bound certifies its optimal precision, and a linear estimate supplies the starting point. This is exactly why reprojection-error minimization is the book's gold standard.
